nature-es-084.title: Nutrient cycles: nature's recycling system
nature-es-084.text: In 1749 Carl Linnaeus wrote about nature's recycling in a book called Oeconomia Naturae, the 'economy of nature'. The phrase fits. A nutrient cycle is the movement of living and non-living matter back into the making of new living matter. Energy and matter behave very differently here. Energy flows one way through an ecosystem and is never reused, while mineral nutrients go round and round. The cycles include carbon, sulfur, nitrogen, water, phosphorus and oxygen, among others. Decomposition, the breakdown of dead matter, largely controls the recycling, and food webs full of different species do the work. Not every ecosystem balances its books. Some run a nutrient debt and act as sinks, while others carry a surplus and act as sources, depending on climate, landform and geology. Most textbooks treat 'nutrient cycle' and 'biogeochemical cycle' as the same thing, though 'nutrient cycle' usually means cycling within one ecosystem. For people, this natural recycling is one of the ecosystem services that sustain human welfare, a supporting service on which much else depends.

nature-es-093.title: Pollination: the courier service behind seeds
nature-es-093.text: Somewhere between 100,000 and 200,000 animal species work as couriers for the world's 250,000 species of flowering plant, and most of them are insects. Their cargo is pollen. Pollination is the moving of pollen from the male part of a flower to the female part, which lets the plant make seeds. Bees, beetles, butterflies, birds and bats carry it, and so do wind and water. About 80% of flowering plants rely on living pollinators. Animal couriers bring a bonus: they allow cross-breeding rather than self-breeding, which keeps plants genetically varied. The economic stakes are large. Three quarters of the plant species that feed the world need pollinators, and insect-pollinated crops are worth over 200 billion dollars. Geography matters too. Farms closer to natural habitat get more pollinator visits and higher crop yields, a regulating service delivered free by the wild land next door.

nature-es-108.title: Food security: enough to eat, every day
nature-es-108.text: In 2020 close to 12% of the world's people, 928 million, were severely food insecure, 148 million more than a year earlier. Food security means reliable access to enough affordable, healthy food. The 1996 World Food Summit put it more fully. All people, at all times, should have physical and economic access to enough safe, nutritious food for an active, healthy life. Hunger often has a surprising cause. It usually stems not from a lack of food but from people being unable to reach the food that exists, most often because they are poor. Nature's services sit under the whole system, and they are fraying. Farming land too hard can trap land in a cycle of falling soil fertility and falling yields, while deforestation and overgrazing degrade land too. Taking too many fish poses serious risks. People rely on fewer and fewer varieties of fewer crop species, and the decline of pollinators could endanger food supplies as well as unbalance ecosystems.

nature-es-110.title: Groundwater recharge: refilling the hidden reservoirs
nature-es-110.text: People move about 24,000 km3 of water a year, roughly double the amount that seeps back into the ground worldwide. That seeping is recharge: the downward movement of water from the surface into underground stores. It is the main way water enters an {{ref:nature-res-112}}, the underground layer of rock or sediment that holds water. Recharge happens naturally through the water cycle, as rain and snowmelt soak in. It also happens artificially, when people route rainwater or reclaimed water underground. What covers the ground makes a big difference. Tree roots help water soak in, while paving, development and logging can strip topsoil, increasing runoff and reducing recharge. Wetlands help hold up the water table, and small wetlands can recharge up to 20% of their volume per season. The rule for sustainable use is simple: over the long run, pumping from such a store should not exceed its recharge. Applying it is harder, because recharge is difficult to measure. Evaporation, water given off by plants and water soaking into soil must all be estimated first.

nature-es-119.title: Storm surge: when the sea walks inland
nature-es-119.text: In 1970 the Bhola cyclone drove a wall of seawater across the Bay of Bengal, killing up to 500,000 people, the deadliest surge on record. A storm surge is a coastal flood of rising seawater pushed ashore by a storm, usually a low-pressure system such as a tropical cyclone. It is measured as the rise above the normal tide, not counting waves. Strong winds piling water toward the coast do most of the work. Low air pressure adds more, lifting the sea about 10 mm for every millibar of pressure drop. The damage outlasts the flood: surges wreck roads and buildings, harm soil fertility, push saltwater inland and spread contaminants. With stronger extreme weather and rising seas from climate change, surges are expected to threaten coastal people more. Nature offers a buffer. Tidal marshes protect coastal habitat from storm surge and flooding.

nature-es-088.title: Biological pest control: hiring a pest's enemies
nature-es-088.text: Around 304 AD, citrus growers in China bought nests of predatory ants to guard their fruit, the first known record of biological pest control. The idea is to use living organisms against pests, whether animals, weeds or disease-causing organisms. It works through predation, parasitism and plant-eating, usually with people actively managing it, and it can form part of {{ref:nature-nbs-283}}. Modern biological control began in the US in the 1870s. State entomologists started handing out parasitoids, insects whose young develop inside or on a host and kill it. Today's agents include lady beetles, parasitoid wasps and flies, and disease organisms such as bacteria, fungi and viruses. Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil bacterium, is the most widely used bacterial agent, and its genes have been put into transgenic crops. The payoff is economic and ecological. Biological control can cut losses from pests, disease carriers and invasive species, and natural enemies used instead of pesticides mean less farm pollution.

nature-es-103.title: Water purification: nature's filter and the engineer's
nature-es-103.text: When New York City's water fell below EPA standards, the city did something unusual. Rather than rely only on treatment plants, it restored its polluted Catskill Watershed and let the land do the cleaning. Water purification is the removal of unwanted chemicals, germs, suspended solids and gases from water so it is fit for a given use. Nature does a great deal of it. Soil and rock layers filter underground water so well that it often needs only a disinfectant added. In bank filtration, natural riverbank sediments provide the first stage of cleaning. Slow sand filters work through living processes rather than simple straining, and a diverse community of water plants helps purify water for human use. Engineered treatment uses physical steps such as filtration and sedimentation, chemical steps such as chlorination, and biological steps. The need is enormous. A 2007 WHO report said 1.1 billion people lacked an improved drinking water supply, and 1.8 million died from diarrheal disease each year.

nature-es-113.title: Microclimates: the weather near the ground
nature-es-113.text: Step from a parking lot into a wooded park and the air changes. A microclimate is the local set of air, soil and water conditions near the ground that differs measurably from its surroundings. It spans a few meters to at most a few kilometers, far smaller than mesoclimates of tens to hundreds of kilometers or macroclimates of hundreds to thousands. Terrain, soil, vegetation, water and buildings shape it by changing sunlight, wind, heat and moisture near the surface. A wooded park stays different from a nearby industrial park because leaves absorb light and heat that roofs and pavement radiate back into the air. That moderating effect has limits: a clearing wider than twice the height of nearby trees loses it. Farmers manage microclimates with irrigation, shade, rows of trees against the wind and plants to shield crops from heat and drought, which matters more as climate extremes grow. Habitat fragmentation can alter microclimates and the biodiversity they support.

nature-es-104.title: Bioprospecting: searching living things for the next drug
nature-es-104.text: Almost one third of the small-molecule drugs approved by the US FDA between 1981 and 2014 were natural products or derived from them. Bioprospecting is the search through living things for molecules and genetic information that could become valuable products such as drugs, cosmetics or farm inputs. Many of today's antibiotics came from it, such as streptomycin from a soil bacterium, and the antimalarial artemisinin came from a plant. Natural molecules are more structurally complex than synthetic ones, so they act on biological targets more precisely. The search now reaches beyond plants and soil microbes to seas, caves, polar regions and extremophiles, organisms that thrive in extreme conditions. It has costs. Over-harvesting prized species can push them toward extinction. The UN and others promote bioprospecting as ethical development built on protecting biodiversity. Critics answer that conservation areas shut local people out of common lands and exploit their knowledge, and the two sides remain at odds.

nature-es-112.title: Medicinal plants: a pharmacy grown for defense
nature-es-112.text: Plants cannot run from insects, fungi or grazing animals, so they make hundreds of chemicals to fight back. Those defenses are why plants work as medicine. Medicinal plants are plants used to keep people healthy or treat illness, in traditional medicine since prehistoric times and in modern medicine today. The Food and Agriculture Organization estimated in 2002 that over 50,000 are used worldwide. Around a quarter of drugs prescribed in modern medicine come from them. By one 2023 estimate the global market was US$68 billion a year, growing 10–20% annually, with China and India leading production and export. In much of the rural developing world, traditional herbal medicine is people's only health care. Yet wild plants face climate change, habitat loss and over-collection. Caution applies too: as of 2015 most plant-based products had not been tested for safety and effectiveness, and natural does not mean safe.

nature-es-116.title: Soil formation: the slowest factory on Earth
nature-es-116.text: In Sicily's Mediterranean climate, weathering makes new soil at about 1/10 mm per year. Soil formation, or pedogenesis, is the slow making of soil, shaped by place, environment and history. It starts with the weathering of fresh parent material, the rock or sediment underneath. Microbes feed on the nutrients released and leave residues that become humus, the dark, stable organic part of soil. Over time the soil develops distinct layers called horizons, which differ in color, structure, texture and chemistry. A full profile takes decades to several thousand years to develop. Farming spends this capital far faster than it is made. Erosion from farm fields is estimated at 11 to 20 times the formation rate on fields farmed without tillage, and over 100 times with conventional tillage. Soil formation is a supporting ecosystem service, and the whole business of feeding people depends on it. Vasily Dokuchaev, regarded as the father of soil science, showed in 1883 that soil forms over time under climate, vegetation, topography and parent material.

nature-es-098.title: Pollinator decline: how worried should anyone be?
nature-es-098.text: A 2021 century-long study found that the number of bee species recorded in 2006–2015 was a quarter lower than before 1990. Pollinator decline is the drop in numbers of insect and other animal pollinators in many ecosystems, recorded since the end of the 20th century. The evidence is strongest in Europe and North America, with similar findings from South America, China and Japan. Managed honey bee colonies fell 25% in Europe (1985–2005) and 59% in North America (1947–2005), though global numbers rose thanks to China and Argentina. The deeper risk is a mismatch. Managed hives grew by 45%, but demand for animal-pollinated crops tripled. About 87.5% of flowering plant species and 60% of crop species use animal pollinators. A 2009 study valued the 100 crops that need them at €153 billion worldwide. Without animal pollination, US farm output is expected to fall by 3 to 8%. Yet so far food production has not suffered: yields of animal-pollinated and other crops have risen at the same rate. Sources disagree on how serious the decline is.

nature-es-094.title: Bees for hire: the market in pollination
nature-es-094.text: Each February around 60% of US bee colonies are trucked to California's Central Valley, where almond trees are about to bloom. Their owners are renting them out. Beekeepers lease honeybee colonies to farmers for a fee, turning crop pollination into a service sold in a market. Honeybees do most pollination of the crops people eat, giving between $235 and $577 billion of benefits to global food production. As of 2016, rentals made up 41% of an average US beekeeper's revenue, their largest source of income. Economists call pollination a positive externality, a benefit that spills over to others, and here the market has managed to pay for it. Almonds dominate, using up to 82% of the pollination market. In 2016 an almond colony earned $165 in rent, about three times other crops, yet once upkeep is counted almond pollination is barely profitable. There is a hidden cost as well. Mixing hives spreads disease to wild bees, a negative externality that reduces biodiversity.

nature-es-107.title: Firewood: the oldest fuel
nature-es-107.text: For most of human history firewood was the main fuel, and the right to gather it was a valued part of many medieval leases. Firewood is any wood burned for fuel, usually as recognizable logs or branches rather than processed pellets. It is renewable, but local demand can quickly outrun how fast trees regrow. Along with clearing land for farming, gathering it is a cause of deforestation, and its smoke causes breathing problems. Moving firewood long distances can also spread tree pests, diseases and invasive species.

nature-es-109.title: The four pillars of food security
nature-es-109.text: Food security is usually broken into pillars. Availability is the supply of food through production, distribution and exchange. Access covers whether food is affordable and how it is shared out, along with people's preferences. Utilization is how well people use the food they get. Stability is the ability to get food over time, since food insecurity can be passing, seasonal or chronic. A further pillar, sustainability, asks that the ways people grow and supply food feed them now without undermining the bases for feeding future generations.

nature-es-085.title: Can anything be recycled forever?
nature-es-085.text: In 1979 {{ref:nature-hist-044}} proposed a 'fourth law' of {{ref:nature-eecon-109}}, saying complete recycling is impossible. Complete recycling would rebuild 100% of waste into new material, forever. {{ref:nature-hist-063}} disagreed. Living systems, he held, can gather chemical elements without limit while energy such as sunlight lasts. The fourth law has been rejected in light of observed recycling in ecosystems. Some authors still say complete recycling is impossible for technological waste, so the dispute lives on there.

nature-es-087.title: Factories versus food webs: two kinds of recycling
nature-es-087.text: Industry recycles only 7% of all plastic waste; the other 93% is presumably left to natural recycling systems. Recycling in human industry differs from recycling in ecosystems in scale, complexity and organization. Industry relies on people and technology, rather than food webs, to turn waste back into marketable goods. Many human 'technoecosystems', systems built around technology, compete with or feed off natural ecosystems.

nature-es-111.title: Managed aquifer recharge: putting water back
nature-es-111.text: A facility in Orange County, California cleans and injects 100 million gallons of water a day underground, or 90 billion gallons a year. That is managed aquifer recharge: deliberately putting water back into underground water stores through altered streambeds, bank filtration, water spreading or recharge wells. It answers a real need. In India, where farmers' over-pumping has drained underground water, the government funded dug-well recharge projects in 100 districts in 2007.

nature-es-095.title: Animals or wind: two ways to move pollen
nature-es-095.text: Biotic pollination uses living animals to carry pollen, while abiotic pollination relies on wind, water or rain. Wind does some 98% of the abiotic work. Relying on it has an advantage: a plant can spend its energy on pollen rather than on showy flowers and nectar to attract animals. Some plants use both, such as an orchid pollinated by rain or by butterflies depending on conditions.

nature-es-096.title: What farming owes to pollinators
nature-es-096.text: Wheat, maize and rice, the main staple grains, are pollinated by wind or by themselves. Many other crops depend on animals. Among the top 15 crops in 2013, slightly over 10% of the human plant diet, 211 of 1916 kcal per person per day, depended on insect pollination. Supply and demand have pulled apart. Managed US beehives fell from close to 6 million after WWII to under 2.5 million, while bee-pollinated crop area grew over 300%. Now about one million hives, nearly half of US honey bees, are trucked to California almond orchards each spring.

nature-es-120.title: Holding back the sea: defenses against storm surge
nature-es-120.text: After the North Sea flood of 1953, engineers built storm-surge barriers that stay open for shipping but close when a surge threatens. The Dutch Delta Works, the Thames Barrier and the Saint Petersburg Dam are among the largest. Barriers are hard infrastructure. Communities can also use soft infrastructure such as dunes or mangroves, better building, and social measures. Warnings, education and local evacuation plans reduce the toll on people.

nature-es-102.title: How seeds travel: on their own or by hitchhiking
nature-es-102.text: The dynamite tree can throw its seeds up to 100 meters. That is self-dispersal, or autochory, where the plant moves its own seeds by gravity or exploding fruit, which limits how far they go. In allochory an outside agent carries them: wind, water or animals, with seeds riding in fur or passing through guts. Humans are agents too. Seeds travel on clothes up to 250 m, on shoes up to 5 km, and in cars sometimes over 100 km.

nature-nbs-285.title: Three ways to deploy natural enemies
nature-nbs-285.text: Biological control comes in three basic strategies. Importation, or classical control, brings a pest's natural enemies into a new place where they did not live before. Early importations were often unofficial, and some introduced species became serious pests themselves. Augmentation adds more predators, parasitoids or microbes when needed. Inoculative release adds a few at intervals to prevent outbreaks. Inundative release adds many at once to knock a pest down fast. The third strategy, conservation, protects the natural enemies already present.

nature-es-090.title: Conservation biological control: feeding the farmer's allies
nature-es-090.text: Nectar plants grown along the borders of rice fields cut planthopper pests 10- to 100-fold. Farmers then sprayed 70% less insecticide and gained 5% in yield. This is conservation biological control: protecting and encouraging the natural enemies of pests that already live in an area. Reshaping cropping systems to favor them is called habitat manipulation, using hedgerows, shelterbelts or beetle banks. In English fields, a meter-wide strip of tussock grass down the middle let aphid predators survive the winter and improved control.

nature-es-091.title: When the cure becomes the pest
nature-es-091.text: In 1935 cane toads were released in Australia to eat cane beetles. They could not reach the beetles, spread fast instead and harmed native frogs and predators. The episode shows the main risk of biological control: an introduced agent can harm biodiversity by attacking native species as well as its target. Vertebrates tend to eat many kinds of food, so they seldom make good control agents, and many classic failures involve them.

nature-es-114.title: Nursery habitats: where the next generation of fish grows up
nature-es-114.text: Seagrass meadows give nursery habitat to over a fifth of the world's 25 largest fisheries, including walleye pollock, the most landed species. A nursery habitat is a place where young marine animals live that contributes more young to the adult population, per unit of area, than other places they use. Mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass are typical. Losing them can mean fewer young reaching adulthood, shrinking populations that both biodiversity and fishing need. Counting crowds of juveniles is not proof enough. The best measure is how much biomass moves from juvenile to adult populations.

nature-es-106.title: Bioprospecting contracts: who shares the profits
nature-es-106.text: Since 1993, when the {{ref:nature-gov-015}} came into force, countries have had the right to control who may use their genetic material. That created a new branch of law. Bioprospecting contracts set the rules for sharing benefits between researchers and the countries whose genetic material they use. They rest on prior informed consent and compensation, and they can bring royalties to poorer countries. Biodiverse countries expect a share rather than letting the discoverer keep the gains privately. Still, not every holder of traditional knowledge is consulted or paid.

nature-es-117.title: CLORPT: the five factors that make a soil
nature-es-117.text: Soil scientists remember five classic factors with one odd word, CLORPT: climate, organisms, relief (the shape of the land), parent material and time. Climate dominates, and soils show the traits of the climate zone where they form. Relief matters because steep slopes lose soil quickly to erosion, so soils there are shallower and less developed than on nearby level ground. Plants hold soil in place and build humus, while animals break down plant matter and mix the soil. Those organisms are astonishingly many: soil is the most species-rich ecosystem on Earth, mostly microbes, many still undescribed.

nature-es-118.title: Jenny's equation: a soil as a sum of its causes
nature-es-118.text: In 1941 Hans Jenny wrote a soil as a function of climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time, leaving room for more factors. Unlike Dokuchaev's earlier equation, his state equation treats time as a factor, adds relief and keeps the list open. It is mostly solved by experiment in the field, varying one factor while holding the others constant. That yields models such as climofunctions and chronofunctions, which trace soil change along climate or time. Soil surveyors worldwide use it as a checklist of what shapes a region's soils.

nature-es-115.title: Pollination management: bringing the bees to the field
nature-es-115.text: A 1950s grower with ten acres of watermelons had wild bees enough. Today's 200-acre grower must bring hives to the field. Pollination management means ensuring a crop's pollination by managing pollinators, pollen-supplying plants and conditions. Growers use honey bees, blue orchard bees, bumblebees, hand pollination and even machines. Bigger single-crop fields make management matter more. The blue orchard bee visits only the target tree and is 100 times more efficient per bee than a honeybee. Pollination limitation, too few pollinators holding back yield, fell by 50% between 1950 and the 2010s, mainly because fields were supplied with managed pollinators.

nature-es-099.title: What is killing the pollinators
nature-es-099.text: Synthetic pesticides, above all neonicotinoids, are a primary driver of pollinator decline, damaging the nerves and immune systems of bees and other pollinators. Other proposed causes include parasites and diseases, habitat destruction, climate change, market forces and competition with invasive species. Some effects are subtle. Air pollution breaks down flower scents so they travel shorter distances, forcing pollinators to fly farther. Climate change can make bees emerge when no plants are flowering. A 2021 global assessment said policy should focus on land-cover change, land management and pesticides.

nature-es-100.title: Pollinators and the vitamins on your plate
nature-es-100.text: An estimated 70% of dietary vitamin A and 55% of folate worldwide come from animal-pollinated crops. Losing pollinators could therefore cut the supply of nutrients that matter for health. A 2015 model found that if all pollinators died off, 71 million more people in low-income countries would lack vitamin A. The same model predicted 1.42 million extra deaths a year, or 700,000 if half of pollinators were lost.

nature-es-081.title: Mangroves: a coastal forest that pays many ways
nature-es-081.text: At least 35 percent of the world's mangroves were destroyed in a single decade, faster than tropical rainforests disappeared. What was lost was a form of natural capital yielding goods and services to coasts, local communities and society at large. Some outputs, such as timber, sell in ordinary markets, where their value shows up as a price. Most do not. Mangroves give nursery habitat to many species, including commercial fish and crustaceans. In Queensland, Australia, an estimated 75 percent of the prawns and fish caught commercially depend on mangroves for part of their life cycle. The forests keep water clean by cycling nutrients and slowing water so sediment settles out. They also take carbon from the air and store it in their wood and waterlogged soils, adding to the coast's {{ref:nature-nbs-034}}. Economic arguments weigh most in mangrove conservation. Yet their true economic value is hard to measure, and key ecological functions are undervalued.

nature-es-121.title: Climate regulation: nature's thermostat
nature-es-121.text: Climate regulation is among the services thought to have no viable substitute. It is the regulating service by which nature dampens environmental change, for example by storing carbon and moderating local temperatures. A 1970 report that coined 'environmental services' already listed it alongside pollination, fisheries and flood control. Tropical rainforests are crucial to it because they capture and store carbon. Mangroves sequester carbon too, coastal seas help regulate climate, and urban trees cool microclimates and take up carbon dioxide. The service can falter. Regime shifts, sudden lasting changes, can weaken it. Examples include forest turning into savanna and faster summer loss of Arctic ice. {{ref:nature-acct-109}} is one attempt to put a money value on regulating services such as this one.

nature-es-083.title: Mangroves as water filters
nature-es-083.text: Runoff from land passes through a series of natural filters: coastal forests first, then mangroves, then seagrass beds, before it reaches coral reefs. Reefs need these buffers to avoid being overgrown by algae. Mangroves trap, remove and recycle nutrients, pollutants and particles. Their roots slow the water so sediment settles, taking bound toxins and nutrients with it. Because wastewater treatment plants are costly, mangroves are often chosen to receive wastewater, and purpose-built mangrove wetlands now treat sewage and fish-farm waste.

nature-es-122.title: Watershed services: what a healthy catchment gives
nature-es-122.text: A healthy catchment, the land that drains into a river or lake, gives water-related benefits: less soil erosion, lower landslide risk and milder floods and droughts. These are watershed, or hydrological, services. They are one of the three main kinds of service sold in payment-for-ecosystem-services schemes, with climate mitigation and biodiversity. Costa Rica's payment scheme explicitly counted hydrological services among its four environmental services. Growing markets for them may reward forests managed with low-impact logging.

openers.provisioning-and-regulating-services: Nature's recycling system moves matter from dead things back into new life, and much of the economy rests on it. This chapter looks at the working services: animals moving pollen so plants can make seeds, rain and snowmelt sinking down to refill underground water, and living organisms keeping pests in check. It also covers what those services deliver, from water fit to drink and medicinal plants to the slow making of soil. Some services guard against disaster, such as coastal defenses against a storm surge, seawater pushed ashore by a storm. And some are faltering: insect and other pollinators have been declining in many ecosystems since the end of the 20th century.

reviews.provisioning-and-regulating-services: Nutrients cycle, pollen travels, water sinks into aquifers and soil builds at a fraction of a millimeter a year, and the economy draws on every step. These services feed people, purify water, temper local climates and supply medicines, firewood and fish raised in mangrove nurseries. Many are priced only indirectly: almond growers rent bees, Orange County injects cleaned water underground, and payment schemes reward healthy watersheds. Others show up only when they fail, as when farm erosion outruns soil formation, cane toads turn on native wildlife, or pollinators decline while demand for their crops triples. Seen together, provisioning and regulating services are less a list of gifts than a working system that people can strengthen or wear down.
